US midterm elections: Voting machines malfunction in New York’s Westchester CountyBy Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
A handful of polling locations across the United States have reported some technical issues with how ballots are cast during the midterm elections, causing officials to delay the closing time for polls so votes can be cast.
In Westchester County, New York, north of New York City, officials said the machines meant to automatically read physical ballots were having trouble because the paper the ballots were printed on was too thick.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Severe weather disrupts election day across several US stateslist 2 of 3Michigan voters face crucial choice as Trump’s grip on Congress is testedlist 3 of 3Texans vote in most expensive Senate race in US historyend of list
Al Jazeera’s Kristen Saloomey, reporting from Tarrytown, New York, said election officials were collecting ballots to be counted later manually. The machines are made by a company called Liberty Vote, a company that used to be called Dominion, which had a rocky history with US President Donald Trump, who had accused it, without evidence, of misrepresenting voting counts in past elections.
“Election officials are reassuring that they will be counted manually after everything is done,” Saloomey said, “and we don’t know of this issue in other districts across New York or the United States, and there are dozens that do use this system.”

Voters fill out their ballots in the US midterm elections in Detroit, Michigan, on November 3, 2026 [Sarah Yenesel/EPA]By Evan SemonesPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
After a full day of voting, the first polls have begun closing in the consequential US midterm elections.
Control of the US Congress is on the line, with all 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats up for grabs.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Voting underway in closely contested US midterm elections 2026list 2 of 3US midterm voting begins in high-stakes test of Trump’s presidencylist 3 of 3How US midterms have cost a record $12bn as cost of living soarsend of list
Democrats, who have campaigned on promises to combat the country’s rising cost of living and end the US-Israel war on Iran, are eyeing a return to power in the US House. The party is also optimistic it could recapture control of the US Senate from Republicans when all ballots are counted.
The first clues to how the midterms may affect each party will appear in the US state of Kentucky’s highly competitive sixth congressional district, where polls closed at 6pm ET (23:00 GMT).
In the conservative district, which includes the state’s second-largest city, Lexington, Democrats have invested heavily in the campaign of US Navy veteran Zach Dembo, who is running against a Trump-backed physician and former state lawmaker, Ralph Alvarado.
If Republicans hold the seat, it could signal how the party may perform in other races across the country.
Results from all of the day’s races will continue to come in throughout Tuesday evening. But some may not be known until Wednesday, or later, as more states finish voting and officials start releasing their vote counts.

Raphinha scores Barcelona's second goal of the November 3 football match [Julian Finney/Getty Images]By AFP and ReutersPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
Raphinha struck twice to propel Barcelona to a 3-0 Champions League win over visitors Aston Villa on Tuesday, ending the English side’s perfect start to the football competition.
Five-time winners Barcelona took an early lead through Lamine Yamal before Raphinha continued his fine goal-scoring form with a second-half brace.
Barca bounced back after defeat to champions Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) in their previous European outing to stay in the hunt for a top-eight league phase berth.
Manager Unai Emery’s Villa competed well in the first half, but were eventually undone by Barca’s greater ability in the final third.
The Champions League anthem was not played before the game, as a mark of respect for Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died of a cardiac arrest on Tuesday morning after an on-pitch collision in a Spanish second-division match the previous day, provoking shock across the football world.
“Yes, it was [a good win]; I want to dedicate this win to the fans, but today I don’t want to talk about football, I want to send a message to the family of Jesus – may he rest in peace,” Raphinha told Movistar.
“This can happen to anyone; it’s very tough … you’re going to play a game, and the same thing can happen to you…
“From the club, I want to send a message of strength to the family.”
Villa captain John McGinn had only visited Camp Nou once previously, on a summer holiday as an eight-year-old, and might have expected better weather than the downpour both teams were subjected to. Advertisement

Voters line up to cast their ballots in the US midterm elections on Election Day, November 3, in Austin, Texas, the United States [Mike Segar/Reuters]By Joseph StepanskyPublished On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
Houston, Texas, the US – Texas voters have begun casting ballots in a consequential US Senate race that has already become the most expensive in United States history.
All told, at least $573.2m had been poured into support for both Republican candidate Ken Paxton and Democratic candidate James Talarico ahead of the Tuesday, November 3 vote.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3What time do polls open and close in the US midterm elections 2026?list 2 of 3In Pictures: US midterm elections in 20 photoslist 3 of 3On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm voteend of list
The figure has included at least $212m to support Paxton from billionaire Elon Musk, whose SpaceX company is based in southern Texas.
The sum made voters of varying political persuasions queasy as they cast their ballots in a race that has been defined by affordability issues.
“That kind of money is being spent on the wrong stuff,” said Rico Sanchez, a 40-year-old union sheet metal worker who voted for Democrats based on the sky-high cost of living.
“It’s about control,” he said.
Kasey Blanco, a 21-year-old who split his ballot, voting for Republican Governor Greg Abbott and Democratic US Senate candidate Talarico, echoed the sentiment.
“It’s kind of scary,” he said. “You see the extent that a lot of these politicians are trying to get into the game and distort the view.”
Political power “should be from the people, by the people”, Blanco said.
The record spending has included both funds raised by the campaigns, as well as outside spending.
